hypotheses.title: claimRefund allows anyone to steal refunds with non-20-byte walletAddress
hypotheses.description: When a refund's walletAddress is not exactly 20 bytes (e.g., Solana/Bitcoin addresses), the receiver defaults to msg.sender. The check `require(bots[msg.sender] || msg.sender == receiver)` then trivially passes for any caller since receiver == msg.sender. Any untrusted actor who knows or can guess the externalId can claim the refund to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A cross-chain swap to Solana/Bitcoin reverts, creating a RefundInfo with a non-20-byte walletAddress. 2) Attacker observes the onRevert/onAbort event (externalId is public) or front-runs. 3) Attacker calls claimRefund(externalId); receiver defaults to msg.sender; require passes. 4) Funds are transferred to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of refunded user funds; any pending refund with a non-EVM address is stealable by any observer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that only the intended recipient (or a bot) can claim; for non-20-byte addresses, gate claims behind bots[] only, or store an explicit authorized claimer.

hypotheses.title: GatewayTransferNative.withdraw is public and callable by anyone
hypotheses.description: Unlike GatewayCrossChain where withdraw is internal, GatewayTransferNative.withdraw is declared `public` with no access modifier. Any external caller can invoke it, causing the contract to call gateway.withdraw with attacker-chosen sender, outputToken, and amount. Since the contract holds user funds and approvals, an attacker can drain any ZRC20 balance held by the contract to an arbitrary recipient.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls withdraw(externalId, attackerBytes, victimToken, contractBalance). 2) Contract invokes gateway.withdraw sending the contract's token balance to the attacker-specified sender. 3) Funds leave the contract to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drainage of any ZRC20 tokens held by GatewayTransferNative.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change visibility to internal (as in GatewayCrossChain) or add onlyGateway/onlyOwner gating.

hypotheses.title: Missing slippage protection on DODO mixSwap output in onCall
hypotheses.description: `_doMixSwap` forwards `params.minReturnAmount` and `params.expReturnAmount` from the user-supplied `swapDataZ` blob directly to DODO's `mixSwap`. Because the entire swap payload is attacker-controlled (it arrives via the cross-chain message), a malicious sender can set `minReturnAmount = 0`, disabling all slippage protection. The contract then withdraws `outputAmount` to the destination chain based on whatever the router returns, so a sandwich/MEV attacker can drain value from the swap.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a cross-chain message with `swapDataZ` encoding `minReturnAmount = 0` and a large `fromTokenAmount`. 2) On `onCall`, `_doMixSwap` executes the swap with no minimum-out. 3) A searcher front-runs the swap on the DODO pool, moving price against the victim, then back-runs. 4) Victim receives far less `outputAmount` than fair value, which is then withdrawn to the destination.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds via sandwich/MEV; the platform fee is computed on the input amount, so the user bears the entire slippage loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a protocol-level minimum-out (e.g., compute expected output via an oracle/TWAP and require `outputAmount >= expected * (1 - maxSlippage)`), or reject `swapData` with `minReturnAmount == 0`.

hypotheses.title: claimRefund deletes refundInfo after external token transfer
hypotheses.description: In `claimRefund`, the state variable `refundInfos[externalId]` is deleted only after `TransferHelper.safeTransfer` performs an external call to the token contract. If the token is a malicious ERC-20 (or a token with a callback such as ERC-777), the recipient's `tokensReceived` hook can re-enter `claimRefund` with the same `externalId` before the `delete` executes, causing the refund to be paid out multiple times.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets a refund recorded in `refundInfos` (e.g., via `onRevert`/`onAbort` with a non-20-byte walletAddress, or by being the receiver). 2) Attacker deploys/uses a token whose `transfer` calls back into the attacker contract. 3) Attacker calls `claimRefund(externalId)`; during `safeTransfer` the token callback re-enters `claimRefund(externalId)`; the require checks still pass because `refundInfos[externalId]` has not been deleted yet. 4) Repeat until contract balance is drained.
hypotheses.impact: Double/multiple spending of the same refund entry, draining the contract's token balance and breaking accounting for other users' refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Delete `refundInfos[externalId]` (or set a claimed flag) before performing the external `safeTransfer`, and use a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: Cross-chain message lacks chain/contract binding; replay across chains/contracts
hypotheses.description: The `onCall` handler trusts the `message` payload (externalId + decoded fields) without verifying that the message originated from the intended source chain, source contract, or that the externalId was actually generated by this protocol. The gateway only enforces `msg.sender == gateway`, but the gateway forwards arbitrary cross-chain messages. An attacker can craft a message with an arbitrary `externalId`, `dstChainId`, `receiver`, `targetZRC20`, and `swapDataZ` and have it delivered via the gateway (e.g., from a chain/contract they control), causing the contract to treat it as a legitimate swap and withdraw funds to attacker-chosen receivers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract on a connected chain that calls the ZetaChain gateway to send a message to `GatewayCrossChain.onCall`. 2) Attacker crafts `message` with a chosen `externalId`, `dstChainId = BITCOIN_EDDY` (or EVM), `receiver = attacker`, `targetZRC20 = <any ZRC20 held by contract>`, and empty swapData. 3) Gateway delivers the call; `onCall` deducts fee, does no swap, and calls `withdraw`/`withdrawAndCall` sending the contract's ZRC20 balance to the attacker's receiver. 4) Repeat to drain balances.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of all ZRC20 balances held by GatewayCrossChain; arbitrary cross-chain withdrawals to attacker-controlled addresses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include and verify source chain ID, source contract address, and a protocol-generated nonce/externalId in the signed/authenticated message; reject messages whose externalId was not produced by this contract (e.g., maintain a mapping of pending externalIds).

hypotheses.title: GatewayTransferNative.onCall trusts arbitrary message; no source authentication
hypotheses.description: `onCall` decodes `externalId` and `DecodedNativeMessage` from the raw message and immediately transfers `amount - platformFeesForTx` (or swapped output) to `decoded.receiver`. There is no check that the message was produced by a legitimate source (chain ID, source contract, or a previously registered externalId). Any cross-chain message routed through the gateway to this contract can specify an arbitrary receiver and target token, and the contract will pay out its own token balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends a cross-chain message via the gateway to `GatewayTransferNative.onCall` with `zrc20` = a token the contract holds, `amount` = balance, `decoded.receiver` = attacker, `decoded.targetZRC20 == zrc20`. 2) `onCall` transfers `amount - fee` to attacker. 3) Repeat for other tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all ZRC20/ETH balances held by GatewayTransferNative.
hypotheses.recommendation: Authenticate the message: verify source chain ID and source contract, and require the externalId to be one this contract previously issued (mapping of pending IDs).

hypotheses.title: Uniswap V2 spot reserves used for gas-fee swap without TWAP
hypotheses.description: `_swapAndSendERC20Tokens` calls `UniswapV2Library.getAmountsIn` which reads current pair reserves (`getReserves`) to compute `amountInMax`. The `slippage` tolerance is applied on top of this spot-derived quote, but the quote itself is manipulable. An attacker can flash-loan the pool, skew reserves, force the contract to swap a much larger `amountInMax` of `targetZRC20` for the fixed `gasFee`, then unwind the flash loan.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `onCall` that will trigger `_swapAndSendERC20Tokens` (targetZRC20 != gasZRC20). 2) Attacker flash-borrows and dumps `targetZRC20` into the Uniswap pair, depressing its price. 3) `getAmountsIn` now returns a much larger `amountsQuote[0]`, so `amountInMax` is inflated. 4) The router swap executes at the manipulated price, consuming far more `targetZRC20` than necessary. 5) Attacker reverses the flash loan and pockets the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Excessive `targetZRC20` spent on gas-fee conversion; the user's `amountsOut` (withdrawn amount) is reduced, causing direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a manipulation-resistant oracle (TWAP or Chainlink) to bound the gas-fee swap, or cap `amountInMax` against an independent price reference rather than the same pool's spot reserves.

hypotheses.title: onRevert in GatewaySend sends funds to attacker-controlled sender
hypotheses.description: `GatewaySend.onRevert` decodes `sender` from `context.revertMessage[32:]` and immediately calls `TransferHelper.safeTransfer(context.asset, sender, context.amount)`. The `revertMessage` is attacker-influenced (it is constructed from user-supplied payloads in `depositAndCall`), and there is no check that the sender matches the original depositor or that the asset/amount correspond to a real pending transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers a cross-chain call that will revert (e.g., by supplying a `targetContract` that reverts or by causing the gateway to call `onRevert`). 2) Attacker controls the `revertMessage` bytes so that `sender` is the attacker's address. 3) Gateway invokes `onRevert`; the contract transfers `context.asset`/`context.amount` to the attacker even though the attacker never deposited those funds.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of any tokens held by `GatewaySend` that the gateway reports as revert assets; attacker can drain contract balances by repeatedly triggering reverts with forged revert messages.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the revert recipient to the original depositor recorded at deposit time (e.g., store `externalId => depositor`), and validate `context.asset`/`context.amount` against that record before transferring.

hypotheses.title: onCall in GatewaySend uses transferFrom on gateway, causing DoS
hypotheses.description: In `onCall`, when `fromToken != _ETH_ADDRESS_`, the code calls `IERC20(fromToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` where `msg.sender` is the gateway. The gateway contract does not hold or approve these tokens for this contract; the tokens were already transferred to this contract by the gateway's deposit flow. This `transferFrom` will revert (no allowance/balance on gateway), causing every inbound ERC20 cross-chain call to fail.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User initiates a cross-chain deposit of an ERC20 token to this contract. 2) Gateway calls `onCall` with `fromToken` as the ERC20. 3) `transferFrom(msg.sender=gateway, ...)` reverts because gateway has no allowance/balance. 4) The entire receive path is broken; user funds are stuck in the gateway's revert flow.
hypotheses.impact: All inbound ERC20 cross-chain receives fail; user funds frozen; protocol unusable for ERC20.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `transferFrom` call; the tokens are already delivered to this contract by the gateway before `onCall` is invoked.

hypotheses.title: onCall in GatewaySend trusts msg.sender as token source for transferFrom
hypotheses.category: Integration / Wrong assumption about external caller
hypotheses.description: In `onCall`, when `fromToken != _ETH_ADDRESS_`, the contract executes `IERC20(fromToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)`. The `msg.sender` here is the GatewayEVM contract, not the original user. The gateway does not hold the user's tokens nor has it approved this contract, so the transferFrom will either revert or pull tokens from the gateway's own balance if it happens to hold any. The intended source should be the gateway's forwarded asset (which the gateway already transferred to this contract) or the recipient encoded in the message.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a cross-chain message with `fromToken` set to an arbitrary ERC20 and `amount` large. 2) GatewayEVM calls `onCall` on GatewaySend. 3) `transferFrom(msg.sender=gateway, address(this), amount)` executes. 4) If the gateway holds any balance of that token (e.g., from other in-flight operations or its own reserves), the attacker drains it into GatewaySend and then forwards it to `evmWalletAddress` chosen by the attacker. 5) Even without a balance, the call reverts and legitimate cross-chain receives are broken.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of any ERC20 balance held by the GatewayEVM contract; alternatively, denial of service for all cross-chain ERC20 receives because the transferFrom always fails.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not use `msg.sender` as the token source. Either rely on the gateway having already transferred the asset to this contract (and skip transferFrom), or use the recipient/sender encoded in the message as the `from` address with proper allowance checks.

hypotheses.title: GatewaySend.onCall trusts gateway-supplied fromToken without verifying deposit
hypotheses.description: onCall is onlyGateway, but the gateway forwards arbitrary user-supplied messages. The function decodes fromToken/toToken/amount from the message and, if fromToken != ETH, calls `IERC20(fromToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` where msg.sender is the gateway. If the gateway has approved this contract (or if fromToken is a malicious token), the attacker can craft a message causing the contract to pull tokens from the gateway or from any address that has approved this contract, then send them to an attacker-controlled recipient.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker initiates a cross-chain call routed through the gateway to GatewaySend.onCall with a crafted message specifying fromToken = victim token, toToken = attacker token, recipient = attacker. 2) onCall executes transferFrom(gateway, this, amount) and then transfers output to attacker. 3) If gateway holds/approves balances or if any user has approved this contract, funds are drained.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens held by or approved to GatewaySend; potential draining of gateway allowances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not trust message-supplied token addresses; validate fromToken against the actual asset delivered by the gateway, and never perform transferFrom from msg.sender (gateway) based on user-controlled data.

hypotheses.title: Fee deducted but swap runs on gross amount in GatewayCrossChain
hypotheses.description: `_handleFeeTransfer` transfers `platformFeesForTx` out of the contract, but `amount` is then reduced by `platformFeesForTx` and passed to `_doMixSwap`. However, `_doMixSwap` in this file (and the DODO proxy) uses `params.fromTokenAmount` from the user-supplied `swapDataZ`, NOT the `amount` argument. If the user sets `fromTokenAmount = amount` (gross), the DODO router will pull the full gross amount while the contract only holds `amount - fee`, causing the swap to revert or, if balance exists, pulling more than intended and mixing fee accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker crafts a message where `params.fromTokenAmount == gross amount`. 2. Fee is transferred out. 3. `_doMixSwap` calls mixSwap with gross fromTokenAmount, which pulls more than the post-fee amount. 4. If contract holds dust from previous txs, the extra is drained; otherwise swaps revert and funds get stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Fee accounting is inconsistent with swap input; contract balance can be drained or swaps stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ignore user-supplied `fromTokenAmount` and always pass the post-fee `amount` to the router; verify `params.fromTokenAmount == amount` explicitly.

hypotheses.title: onCall in GatewaySend has no refund/fee accounting and can be drained
hypotheses.description: When `fromToken != toToken`, `_doMixSwap(swapData)` uses `params.fromTokenAmount` from user-supplied `swapData`. If the user encodes `fromTokenAmount` larger than the `amount` held from the gateway, the swap pulls additional tokens from `GatewaySend`'s own balance (which may hold other users' pending deposits) or reverts. Also, `_doMixSwap` uses `msg.value` for ETH swaps, but the ETH held in the contract from previous deposits can be consumed here.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sends message with `fromTokenAmount` inflated. 2. `_doMixSwap` pulls extra from contract's token balance (other users' pending funds). 3. Attacker receives output; other users lose deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of other users' pending cross-chain funds; insolvency of GatewaySend.
hypotheses.recommendation: Override `params.fromTokenAmount` with the received `amount` before calling `_doMixSwap`, and account for `msg.value` explicitly.

hypotheses.title: Missing deadline/expiry check on user-supplied DODO swap deadline
hypotheses.description: `params.deadline` is taken verbatim from the attacker-controlled `swapDataZ` and passed to `IDODORouteProxy.mixSwap`. There is no check that `deadline >= block.timestamp` or that it is within a sane window. A malicious sender can set `deadline = 0` (or a past timestamp), which some routers interpret as "no deadline", allowing the swap to be executed much later at an unfavorable price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a cross-chain message with `deadline = 0`. 2) The message is queued and executed by the gateway at a later time when pool prices have moved adversely. 3) `mixSwap` executes with no effective deadline, filling at the worse price. 4) Victim's `outputAmount` is reduced.
hypotheses.impact: User receives less output than expected due to delayed execution at stale prices.
hypotheses.recommendation: Override `params.deadline` with `block.timestamp + MAX_DEADLINE` (or reject if `params.deadline < block.timestamp`).

hypotheses.title: onCall in GatewaySend transfers to arbitrary recipient before state finalization
hypotheses.description: `GatewaySend.onCall` performs `IERC20(fromToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` and then `_doMixSwap` / `IERC20(toToken).transfer(evmWalletAddress, outputAmount)` with no reentrancy protection and no state update ordering. A malicious `fromToken`/`toToken` (or DODO route proxy) can re-enter `onCall` or `depositAndCall` while the contract still holds funds, and the recipient is fully attacker-controlled via the decoded `recipient` bytes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a cross-chain message whose `recipient` is the attacker and whose `fromToken`/`toToken` is a malicious ERC-20 with a callback. 2) Gateway calls `onCall`; during `transferFrom` or `transfer`, the malicious token re-enters `onCall` with a second crafted message. 3) Because there is no nonReentrant guard and no per-message state, the second call also succeeds, moving additional contract-held tokens to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens held by `GatewaySend` (including tokens belonging to other in-flight cross-chain messages), leading to insolvency for other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` guard to `onCall` and validate that `fromToken`/`toToken` are whitelisted or that the swap target is trusted; avoid transferring to arbitrary recipients before all state is settled.
